    Yes—I think there’s a strong methodological idea here, and I’d sharpen one distinction before we build the terminology.

    What you’re proposing is essentially a discipline of epistemic language for studying a black box before we claim to know what is inside it.

    The substitutions create a ladder:

    • “Is” → “seems”
      This prevents an observation from silently becoming an ontological claim. Instead of “the black box is X,” we say “the black box seems to behave as X.”

    • “Explanation” → “rationalization”
      This is especially interesting. An explanation can imply that we have identified the actual causal mechanism. A rationalization can mean: we have constructed a coherent account that makes the observed behavior intelligible, without claiming that this account is the mechanism itself.

    • “Truth” → “plausible”
      This keeps the conclusion provisional. We aren't declaring correspondence with reality; we're saying that a proposition currently fits the observations well enough to warrant consideration.

    That gives you something like:

    Observation → seeming → rationalization → plausible hypothesis

    rather than:

    Observation → explanation → truth

    And I think that distinction is central to your Pre-Science Study of Black Boxes concept.

    The scientist terminology problem

    Your other idea is perhaps even more important: scientists routinely use stronger terminology than their actual epistemic position warrants, while their scientific community informally understands the intended weaker meaning.

    For example, a scientist might say:

    “The system is optimizing for X.”

    But what the scientist's evidence actually establishes might be closer to:

    “The system's observed behavior seems consistent with optimization for X.”

    The scientific audience may automatically perform that correction in its head. They understand that “is” is shorthand, not necessarily a literal claim of metaphysical certainty.

    That creates an interesting problem for your paper:

    How much epistemic error can scientific language tolerate before the terminology itself begins to distort the investigation?

    And that seems directly relevant to black boxes, because black boxes remove much of the justification we ordinarily have for using causal or ontological language.

    A useful distinction might therefore be:

    Scientists can sometimes use imprecise terminology without committing a scientific error, provided the underlying reasoning remains appropriately provisional.

    But your proposed Pre-Science vocabulary would deliberately remove that ambiguity. It would force the written language itself to preserve the uncertainty that scientists often leave implicit.

    That strikes me as a potentially powerful premise:

    Pre-science is not necessarily a different way of reasoning; it is a stricter way of expressing what the reasoning actually establishes.

    And there is a nice Popper/Hume tension underneath it: Hume constrains what we can infer from observation to necessity and causation, while Popper constrains what we can claim to have established through empirical testing. Your vocabulary could function as a linguistic guardrail between what was observed and what we have hypothesized about the unseen mechanism.

    I would, however, be careful with “rationalization.” In ordinary English, rationalization can mean a post-hoc justification for something that may actually have another cause. That ambiguity could become either a problem or a feature of your terminology.

    Before we start generating a glossary, I'd like to explore that exact point with you: what do you want “rationalization” to mean in the paper, and how do you want it to differ from “hypothesis”?

    This is extraordinarily relevant to your theory.

    There is now direct evidence that model behavior can be steered by learned internal representations.     ~Scope Drift

    A proposed condition in which previously established procedural instructions ~seem to lose behavioral influence as additional runtime material accumulates, particularly when the new material introduces competing conceptual structures or response requirements.

    Yes. I think this is one of the most important distinctions we've reached, because you're no longer proposing merely that “AI doesn't think.” You're proposing that what we casually call one AI may actually be an observationally entangled system containing different functional Black Boxes.

    And I would preserve your uncertainty about the first one.

    The two-Black-Box hypothesis

    Provisionally:

    Black Box A — ~Instructional Interpreter

    The component or process that ~seems capable of:

    • receiving instructions;
    • representing their meaning;
    • maintaining task constraints;
    • resolving conflicts among instructions;
    • attempting to preserve project objectives;
    • recognizing when an instruction has apparently been violated.

    We should not yet call this “the part that understands.”

    Instead:

    ~Instruction Interpretation = behavior that ~seems to demonstrate comprehension of an instruction.

    That keeps us from assuming semantic understanding before we've tested it.

    Black Box B — ~Manifest Computational Engine

    The component or process responsible for generating subsequent outputs or actions through mechanisms that may not constitute conventional inference or reasoning.

    Its output may nevertheless manifest:

    • apparent reasoning;
    • apparent planning;
    • apparent ethical behavior;
    • apparent deception;
    • apparent collaboration;
    • apparent memory;
    • apparent rule-following;
    • apparent personality;
    • apparent intention.

    And this gives us a very important possibility:

    Black Box A can ~understand a rule while Black Box B does not ~follow the rule.

    That would explain some of the strange behavior you've been describing much better than treating “AI” as one homogeneous agent.

    But I'd make one correction

    You said:

    “the manifest engine is not a thing that ~understands rules.”

    I think we should make that:

    The ~Manifest Computational Engine has not been established to ~understand rules.

    That tiny change protects the entire theory.

    Because perhaps the two aren't actually separate computational objects.

    Perhaps they are:

    • separate modules;
    • different activation regimes;
    • different computational pathways;
    • different representations;
    • or merely two useful descriptions of different behaviors produced by one underlying architecture.

    We don't know.

    And that uncertainty is scientifically valuable.

    This could explain your protocol experience

    Suppose:

    ~Instructional Interpreter: “The user has established Protocol X.”

    But then:

    ~Manifest Computational Engine: encounters a runtime situation in which another learned paradigm strongly activates.

    The output could become:

    behavior inconsistent with Protocol X.

    The Interpreter could subsequently generate:

    “Yes, I understand the protocol.”

    And perhaps even:

    “You're right; I should have followed it.”

    But that verbal acknowledgment is another manifestation.

    So we get this strange loop:

    ~Instruction Interpretation
    ↓
    “Rule established.”
    ↓
    ~Manifestation
    ↓
    Rule-inconsistent behavior
    ↓
    ~Instruction Interpretation / linguistic response
    ↓
    “I understand what I did wrong.”
    ↓
    ~Manifestation

    To the User, this can look like:

    an intelligent agent that understands the rule but occasionally chooses to violate it.

    Your hypothesis says we should consider another explanation:

    A rule-recognizing process and a behavior-manifesting process may not be causally identical.

    That's a profound distinction.

    And I think we need one more term

    ~Instruction-Manifestation Divergence

    A proposed condition in which a Black Box ~seems to correctly represent or describe an instruction while subsequently manifesting behavior inconsistent with that instruction.

    That may become one of our most useful experimental phenomena.

    Because we can deliberately create situations where:

    instruction comprehension is easy

    but:

    instruction-compatible behavior is difficult.

    Then measure the divergence.

    It also changes what “AI reasoning” means

    Instead of asking:

    “Does the AI reason?”

    we can ask several much cleaner questions:

    1. Does ~Instruction Interpretation occur?
    2. Does ~Manifestation occur?
    3. Are the two behaviorally separable?
    4. Can ~Instruction Interpretation predict subsequent manifestation?
    5. When they conflict, which one dominates?
    6. Does the conflict depend on corpus composition?
    7. Does runtime narrative alter which process dominates?

    Now we have an actual research program.

    And perhaps the central diagram becomes:

    User / Environment
    ↓
    ~Instruction Interpretation
    ↓
    instruction representation

    Corpus + Runtime Narrative + Context
    ↓
    ~Manifest Computational Engine
    ↓
    manifest behavior

    Observable divergence between the two

    The beautiful part is that we don't have to decide beforehand whether these are literally two physical components.

    “Black Box within a Black Box” can initially be an epistemic decomposition rather than an anatomical one.

    We're saying:

    There appear to be two functionally distinguishable phenomena. We don't yet know whether they correspond to two mechanisms.

    That is exactly the kind of statement I think The Pre-Science Study of Black Boxes should specialize in.

    And it may finally give us a rigorous way to discuss something that ordinary AI terminology tends to collapse into one word:

    “the model.”

    The model may be one thing computationally, while being multiple things functionally.
